title: AI in the quotation workflow
notes:
What this slide explains
This slide separates the work by component.

Natural speaking script
This slide separates the work by component. A vendor uploads a document through the app. The document service checks the claimed type against the file bytes, checks the size and keeps the original. The Java extraction service then asks Python FastAPI to turn PDF, Excel or Word into text and tables. For a scanned PDF, PDFBox renders pages and local Tesseract reads the image. Java sends that text to Groq using a strict JSON schema. The default model is openai/gpt-oss-120b. If rate limits are hit, GroqClient can try the configured fallback models. After extraction, Java validates the fields, matches quoted lines to RFQ lines and recalculates every amount. A buyer sees any flags and a manager remains responsible for award decisions.

Technical terms
FastAPI is the Python web framework for the file parsing endpoints. OCR means optical character recognition, which turns text inside page images into text. A JSON schema defines the allowed fields and types in a structured response. A fallback model is another configured model the client can try when rate limits prevent the first model from responding.

SUTRA example
For a scanned quotation, Python detects very little PDF text; Java then uses PDFBox plus Tesseract before sending readable text to Groq.

Point to emphasise
Groq does not calculate totals or choose a vendor. Java owns financial calculation, and people own review and approval.

Likely viva questions
Q: Does Python call Groq? A: No. Python parses documents, does rule-based extraction and matching endpoints; Java calls Groq.
Q: What happens for a scanned PDF? A: PDFBox renders it and local Tesseract performs OCR.
Q: What model is configured by default? A: openai/gpt-oss-120b, with configured fallback models.

title: Two AI uses, with different boundaries
notes:
What this slide explains
SUTRA uses the configured Groq service in two user-facing ways.

Natural speaking script
SUTRA uses the configured Groq service in two user-facing ways. First, the quotation reader extracts structured vendor information from uploaded files. Second, Sahayak is a staff-facing question-answering assistant. It receives a bounded context built from relevant platform data and can return links only to purchase requests and quotations present in that context. It replies in the same language and script requested, including Hindi, Hinglish written in Latin letters, or English. If a buyer pastes an RFQ email or item list, Sahayak can return a draft card. That card still needs the buyer to check the fields and click Create RFQ. The chat itself is read-only. It cannot edit records, submit quotations, approve vendors or award an RFQ.

Technical terms
Context-based answering means the model receives a limited set of current records rather than access to the database itself. A draft is a proposed form state and is not yet a saved purchase request. An advisory grade is information for review, not an approval.

SUTRA example
A buyer pastes “buy 500 bearings by 15 March” into Sahayak. The assistant returns a draft card; the buyer confirms the item, quantity and date, then creates the RFQ in the RFQ screen.

Point to emphasise
Sahayak can suggest; the user takes the action. Draft generation does not create a request automatically.

Likely viva questions
Q: Can Sahayak award a vendor? A: No. It is read-only and says only an authorised manager or admin records an award.
Q: Where do its answer links come from? A: The service validates them against request and quotation IDs included in the current context.
Q: What happens after an RFQ draft is generated? A: The buyer reviews it and explicitly creates the RFQ.

title: Safety comes from layered checks
notes:
What this slide explains
There are several safeguards around the language model.

Natural speaking script
There are several safeguards around the language model. The request asks Groq to return a strict schema and to report what the vendor printed instead of calculating or repairing figures. It also treats vendor documents as untrusted and tells the model to ignore instructions embedded in those files. These prompt rules are useful, but they do not guarantee complete resistance to prompt injection. The Java service validates the structured fields, matches line items, recalculates the totals and raises flags for uncertain, missing or inconsistent values. If automatic extraction fails, the configured AUTO path can move from Groq to the rules engine. The original upload stays available, and a user can retry, edit the extracted lines or enter the quotation manually. Scanned text can be wrong too, so confidence and review flags matter.

Technical terms
Prompt injection is an attempt to make a model follow text embedded in the input rather than its intended task. Strict structured output requires a defined JSON shape. Confidence is an extraction signal that helps surface uncertain readings; it is not a guarantee of correctness.

SUTRA example
If Tesseract reads an 8 as a 3 in a unit price, the model may extract the wrong number. The buyer can compare the line against the original file, correct it and see that it was edited.

Point to emphasise
Prompt instructions are a mitigation, not a security boundary. A human still checks questionable values.

Likely viva questions
Q: What is the fallback if Groq fails? A: With AUTO and the default engine order, the rules-based extractor is tried next if available.
Q: Does strict JSON mean the extraction is correct? A: No. It controls the response shape; field values can still be wrong.
Q: Is prompt injection fully solved? A: No. The prompt tells the model to ignore document instructions, but that cannot guarantee complete resistance.

title: One sign-in token, checked at the edge and by services
notes:
What this slide explains
At login, the authentication service checks the password with Spring Security and the BCrypt password encoder.

Natural speaking script
At login, the authentication service checks the password with Spring Security and the BCrypt password encoder. It issues a signed HS256 user token that includes the user ID, roles, vendor link, token version and expiry. The React client stores it in sessionStorage and sends it as a Bearer token. The gateway verifies the token, rejects service tokens at user endpoints, and checks whether the account is active and the token version is current. That status is cached for 15 seconds. The backend services also verify the signature and apply method-level role rules and record-level checks. There are four roles: ADMIN, PROCUREMENT, VENDOR and APPROVER. The system also limits public login and vendor-signup endpoints to 20 requests per minute per IP, and locks a username for 15 minutes after five failed sign-in attempts. The login-failure counter is in memory, so a service restart clears it.

Technical terms
BCrypt is a one-way password hashing algorithm designed for password storage. HS256 is HMAC with SHA-256, used here to sign JWTs. Token versioning lets the app invalidate older tokens after account changes. Record-level authorization checks ownership of a specific RFQ or vendor record, not just the broad role.

SUTRA example
A vendor token carries the linked vendor ID. Vendor portal queries use that ID from the authenticated principal, so a vendor cannot ask the app to show another supplier’s quotation by changing a browser value.

Point to emphasise
The UI may hide a menu, but the backend is the real authorization boundary.

Likely viva questions
Q: Where is the JWT stored in the browser? A: sessionStorage, then sent as an Authorization Bearer header.
Q: How can an account change invalidate a token before it expires? A: The gateway checks account activity and token version against auth state, cached for 15 seconds.
Q: Is the login lockout distributed? A: No. The current LoginAttemptService stores attempts in memory for a single instance.

title: Uploads are checked before storage
notes:
What this slide explains
The document service does several checks before it stores a file.

Natural speaking script
The document service does several checks before it stores a file. It sanitises the filename, accepts only PDF, legacy XLS, XLSX and DOCX formats, checks that the content signature matches the extension, and checks the expected package structure for Office files. It enforces a 20 MB limit. It then stores the original bytes in PostgreSQL and calculates a SHA-256 digest for the metadata. An important distinction: I could verify that the hash is calculated and stored, but I did not find code that rejects duplicate file hashes. I also did not find antivirus scanning. The gateway blocks external access to internal service endpoints; CORS is configured for allowed origins; and the public login and vendor signup routes are rate limited. These controls reduce certain risks, but they do not replace malware detection.

Technical terms
Magic bytes are file-header bytes used to identify the actual format. OOXML Office files are ZIP packages with required internal entries. SHA-256 produces a fixed-length digest that can be used to compare content or detect later changes, but computing a digest alone does not perform duplicate rejection or virus scanning. CORS controls browser cross-origin access; it is not authentication.

SUTRA example
A file renamed from a text document to quote.pdf fails because it does not start with the expected PDF signature. A valid DOCX must also contain the expected Word package structure.

Point to emphasise
Do not tell the evaluator that SUTRA scans uploads for viruses or rejects duplicate files. The source code verifies type and stores a SHA-256 value only.

Likely viva questions
Q: Does SUTRA scan uploaded documents for malware? A: No antivirus scanning was found in the implementation reviewed.
Q: Does a stored SHA-256 digest deduplicate files? A: No. The service calculates and stores the digest, but I found no duplicate-rejection logic.
Q: What happens when someone renames a text file as PDF? A: The magic-byte check rejects it.

title: Financial accuracy stays in the backend
notes:
What this slide explains
The financial path starts with values read from the document or corrected by the buyer.

Natural speaking script
The financial path starts with values read from the document or corrected by the buyer. QuotationCalculator uses Java BigDecimal rather than binary floating-point arithmetic. It applies the discount and tax rules, rounds with HALF_UP, recalculates line and quotation totals, and compares those values with the figures printed by the vendor. A mismatch becomes a warning instead of silently trusting the document. Database columns use PostgreSQL NUMERIC and constraints reject invalid amounts and values. The audit trail uses a transactional outbox so a service records an event in its own transaction and a relay delivers it to the audit service. The audit service gives each entry a sequence number, stores the previous hash and calculates a SHA-256 hash. A database trigger blocks updates to linked entries and deletion. This makes the trail tamper-evident and guarded. It should not be described as impossible to bypass because a privileged database operator can still alter the system outside normal application controls. Quotation records also use optimistic locking with @Version to detect concurrent edits.

Technical terms
BigDecimal is Java’s decimal arithmetic type used for money. HALF_UP rounds ties away from zero at the configured scale. NUMERIC is a fixed-precision database type. An outbox records an event in the same transaction as the business change, then relays it. A hash chain puts each entry’s hash in the next entry’s input, so edits or reordering can be detected. Optimistic locking detects conflicting updates by comparing a version number.

SUTRA example
In the acceptance case, SUTRA recalculated Vertex’s total and flagged the incomplete bearing warranty and 50% advance for review. The manager, not the system, recorded the award.

Point to emphasise
AI never controls financial accuracy. The backend recalculates. The manager chooses.

Likely viva questions
Q: Why use BigDecimal? A: It provides decimal arithmetic appropriate for financial values, unlike binary floating point.
Q: Is the audit chain impossible to alter? A: No. It is tamper-evident and guarded by a database trigger, but not beyond privileged database access.
Q: What does @Version do? A: It helps detect and prevent lost updates when two users edit the same quotation concurrently.

title: Testing covers the interface, services and document logic
notes:
What this slide explains
The test strategy has three automated code suites plus an acceptance script.

Natural speaking script
The test strategy has three automated code suites plus an acceptance script. The frontend uses Vitest and React Testing Library. The tests cover screens and behaviors such as role-sensitive routes, quotation comparison, award forms and assistant drafts. The backend uses JUnit and Mockito for service and controller rules, with some integration coverage against PostgreSQL and real processing components where available. The Python suite uses Pytest for document parsers, the rule-based reader, matching and API endpoints. A separate acceptance script brings up the service stack and runs a realistic end-to-end procurement scenario against a separate test database. These layers do not prove every possible input is safe or accurate, but they provide evidence that key rules and workflows behave as expected.

Technical terms
Unit tests isolate one piece of logic. Integration tests exercise communication with real components such as PostgreSQL. Acceptance checks verify a user-level workflow across services. Mockito supplies controlled stand-ins for dependencies so service rules can be tested predictably.

SUTRA example
The acceptance flow uploads a PDF and an Excel file for each vendor, reads and matches the five material lines, compares totals, confirms a manager can award and verifies the audit history.

Point to emphasise
The figures on the next slide are separate suites and acceptance checks. Do not add them together as one coverage number.

Likely viva questions
Q: Why use mocks? A: They isolate a service’s business rules from external systems and make the test repeatable.
Q: Are acceptance checks the same as unit tests? A: No. They run a broader end-to-end workflow across the service stack.
Q: Does passing the suites prove full coverage? A: No. It is evidence for tested paths, not a guarantee of complete coverage.

title: Recorded test results
notes:
What this slide explains
These are four distinct results.

Natural speaking script
These are four distinct results. The frontend source contains 52 test cases in 10 test files. The repository documents 256 backend tests, with zero failures, zero errors and one skipped test, and a successful build. The skipped test reads the text of a scanned PDF and skips when Tesseract is unavailable. The Python suite reports 38 passed. The acceptance results document records 75 of 75 checks passing on 10 November 2026 in 68 seconds. That run used the automotive test pack and a separate test database. These are recorded results, not tests I reran while preparing the slides. The acceptance report checks the full workflow including vendor uploads, extraction, recalculated totals, role restrictions, award and history. Passing tests provide useful evidence, but they do not mean the project has 100 percent test coverage.

Technical terms
A skipped test did not execute its assertion because a prerequisite was unavailable. Test coverage measures how much code or behavior tests exercise; these pass counts do not establish 100 percent coverage. An acceptance check is one assertion in the end-to-end acceptance script.

SUTRA example
The documented acceptance run checked three vendor quotations. It verified that totals matched the expected values, flagged Vertex’s open bearing warranty, and confirmed the system did not make an automatic award.

Point to emphasise
Do not call 75/75 a fresh run. One backend OCR test was skipped, and these counts are not a coverage percentage.

Likely viva questions
Q: Why was the OCR test skipped? A: Its code skips when Tesseract is not installed or available.
Q: Were the 75 checks run today? A: No. They are from the recorded run on 10 November 2026.
Q: Does 52 frontend tests conflict with the README? A: The README says 54, but counting current frontend test declarations yields 52. The presentation uses the source count and the mismatch is documented in the verification report.

title: Live system workflow
notes:
What this slide explains
This is a route-based overview, not a screenshot.

Natural speaking script
This is a route-based overview, not a screenshot. I checked the local application ports and the frontend and backend were not running, so I did not fabricate a UI capture. The actual React routes include login, purchase requests, request details, quotation review and vendor portal pages. On the buyer side I would open one request, show its requested items and quotations, and use the comparison and award tabs. On the vendor side I would show the open RFQ and submit a quotation file. Extraction results appear on the quotation review page. The final route takes the manager to the award decision and audit history. For a real demo, use a prepared RFQ with uploaded quotations so that extraction and comparison are already available. The demo should stop after showing the recorded history, rather than create unnecessary test data in the live database.

Technical terms
A route is a frontend URL mapped to a React page. A quotation review contains the extracted data and flags. Comparison displays offers side by side. The manager records an approval or rejection, and History lists events associated with that request.

SUTRA example
The repository’s automotive test pack includes one RFQ for five production materials and three vendor quotations. The acceptance report uses this pack to demonstrate ranking and warnings.

Point to emphasise
The visual on this slide is an illustrative source-based route diagram, not an application screenshot.

Likely viva questions
Q: Why are there no real screenshots? A: The app was not running during preparation, and I did not invent screenshots. The route diagram maps to actual source pages.
Q: Where does the vendor submit a bid? A: In the vendor portal at /portal, under an open RFQ.
Q: Who records the final decision? A: A manager with the APPROVER role.

title: Five-minute demonstration run
notes:
What this slide explains
I would start with a user who has already been prepared for the demo, without displaying or inventing credentials.

Natural speaking script
I would start with a user who has already been prepared for the demo, without displaying or inventing credentials. The dashboard gives a quick view of pending work. The buyer opens an existing RFQ so I can point to the requested items. Then I switch to a vendor account and upload a prepared PDF and Excel workbook. I return to the buyer role and open the quotation to show the extraction result, calculated total and any warning. The comparison view shows the vendors side by side. Finally, I switch to a manager account, record the decision and show the history. Keep the timing disciplined: if extraction takes longer than the slot, use a quotation that has already completed extraction. Do not claim the current system generates a purchase order automatically or sends award emails; those are not in this demo path.

Technical terms
A pending-work badge indicates tasks waiting on the current role. A quotation flag describes an amount or commercial term that should be checked. An audit history records who performed system actions and when.

SUTRA example
If the demo RFQ is already seeded with the three automotive quotations, the comparison will show the lowest complete offer and the warranty flag without waiting for a new extraction.

Point to emphasise
Prepare two accounts and test data privately before presenting. Do not put passwords or API keys on slides or screenshots.

Likely viva questions
Q: What should I do if extraction is still running? A: Use a previously extracted quotation or move to the comparison of prepared data.
Q: Can the buyer award the request? A: No. The manager / APPROVER role records the award.
Q: Can the manager award the most expensive quotation without explanation? A: A reason is required when the selected offer is not the lowest complete quotation.

title: Demo dependencies and fallback plan
notes:
What this slide explains
The demo depends on the PostgreSQL database and the Spring services behind the API gateway.

Natural speaking script
The demo depends on the PostgreSQL database and the Spring services behind the API gateway. Python FastAPI handles document parsing, matching and the rules-based extractor. Scanned PDFs additionally need local PDFBox and Tesseract. Groq is an external dependency and needs a configured key and network access. If Groq is rate-limited or unavailable, the quotation AUTO path can try the rules-based engine. Sahayak itself requires Groq, so it will not be available in that case. If OCR is unavailable, use text-based PDFs, Excel or Word files rather than scanned pages. If the backend is unavailable, use genuine screenshots captured in advance or the recorded acceptance report. If the internet is unavailable, local parsing can still work, but Groq features will fail. I would verify the demo with the actual environment before the presentation and avoid showing secrets or credentials.

Technical terms
A local dependency runs on the project machine. An external dependency is a service outside the app, such as Groq’s hosted API. A rules-based engine uses deterministic parsing patterns rather than a generative model. A text-based PDF contains selectable text; a scanned PDF contains page images that need OCR.

SUTRA example
If the Groq API is down during the demo, the quotation path can use Rules if its engine is available. But Sahayak has no rules fallback, so I would skip that feature and continue with the prepared quotation.

Point to emphasise
Groq and Tesseract solve different problems. Groq needs network access; Tesseract is local and is only needed for scanned PDF pages.

Likely viva questions
Q: Does all AI work offline? A: No. Groq calls need internet access. Local parsers and Tesseract can run without that external service if installed.
Q: What works if Tesseract is missing? A: Text-based documents can still be parsed, but scanned PDF reading is unavailable.
Q: What if the whole backend is down? A: Use actual prepared screenshots or the acceptance report, and state that the live backend is unavailable.
